title: Design match ticket booking
dek: Zotato Live opens sales for India vs Pakistan at noon: 1 lakh seats, 50 lakh people. Let them in without falling over, never sell a seat twice, and be fair to the people who aren't bots.

items: See the stands and how many seats are left in each block.
Pick a block and how many seats (up to 4); get seats together, held while you pay.
Pay and get a ticket with a QR code; scan it at the gate.
Join a line when sales open and see your place in it.
Out of scope here: resale between fans, dynamic pricing, and season passes.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: A seat is sold once, never twice
Arriving a second early doesn't beat everyone else; bots don't win on speed
The line keeps working even if booking slows down; nobody sees an error page at 12:00
1 lakh seats, 50 lakh people in the first minutes

items: Orders: 1 lakh seats at about 3 per order is roughly 30,000 orders. The whole sale is small.
Crowd: 50 lakh people refreshing every few seconds is over 10 lakh requests a second at 12:00. No booking system should see that.
Shopping: picking seats and paying takes about 3 minutes. To keep 20,000 people shopping at once, admit 20,000 every 3 minutes, about 110 a second.
So the seats are gone in about 5 minutes of admissions, and 49 lakh people need a fast, honest "sold out".
Writes: 30,000 orders × 3 seats over 5 minutes is about 300 seat updates a second. One database handles that; the risk is everyone fighting over the same rows, not the volume.
Event: `id`, `venue`, `sale_opens_at`, `limit_per_account`.
Seat: `event_id`, `seat_id` (block, row, number), `state` (available, held, sold), `order_id`, `hold_until`.
Order: `id`, `account_id`, `seats`, `state`, `amount`. Ticket: `order_id`, `seat_id`, a signed QR code, `scanned_at`.
Line token: `event_id`, `account_id`, `position`, `admitted_at`, signed by the server.

body.label: API

body.cap: 50 lakh people join the line before noon and get random places. The waiting room admits about 110 a second, only as fast as booking can serve, so about 20,000 shop at once. Each holds seats, pays, and gets a ticket; everyone else sees their place, then "sold out" when the seats are gone.

body.x: The waiting room is the only part that meets the whole crowd, so make it cheap: a static page from a CDN, a signed token, and a small service that answers "where am I in the line?" from memory. Booking sits behind it and only ever sees admitted shoppers. If booking slows down, lower the admit rate; the line just moves slower.

body.name: First try
body.what: Show the seat as free, let the customer pick it, then mark it sold when they pay.
body.use: Simple, and fine for a small theatre on a quiet day.
body.avoid: Hundreds of people see seat N2-14-7 free at the same moment, pick it, and pay. Everyone but one gets a refund and an angry message.
body.ex: At 12:00:10, 300 people tap the same front-row seat behind the bowler's arm.
body.like: Selling tickets from a chart nobody updates until the end of the day.

body.name: Better
body.kind: LOCK THE ROW WHILE THEY PAY
body.what: Lock the seat rows in the database from choosing until payment finishes.
body.use: Nobody else can take the seats in the meantime.
body.avoid: Payment takes a minute or more. Locks held that long block everyone else touching those rows, and a closed app leaves them locked until a timeout.
body.ex: One customer goes to find a card; three others wait on the same block's rows.
body.like: Keeping the till open while a customer runs to the ATM.

body.name: Best
body.what: In one short transaction, move every requested seat from available (or held but expired) to held, with `hold_until` 10 minutes ahead. If fewer rows changed than seats asked for, roll back. Payment changes held to sold, only if the hold is still yours and not expired.
body.use: Exactly one buyer wins each seat, no lock lasts more than a few milliseconds, and seats from people who walk away come back by themselves.
body.avoid: Expired holds must be ignored everywhere, so every query checks `hold_until`, and a sweeper resets them so the counts stay right.
body.ex: Three seats asked, three rows changed: held till 12:13:05. Two changed: someone took one first; roll back and try the next 3 seats together in the block. Only when none are left, show "only 2 left together".
body.like: A coat-check ticket: the coat is yours while the ticket is valid, then it goes back on the rack.

body.cap: A seat is available, held or sold. A hold moves it to held for 10 minutes; payment moves it to sold; no payment by the deadline puts it back. Every move is one conditional update, so two buyers can't both win.

body.x: Fewer fights over the same seats

items: Let customers choose a block and a count, and pick the seats for them. Thousands choosing "the best seat" by hand all collide; assigning from the block spreads them out. Pick candidate seats with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so buyers who arrive together take different seats instead of failing each other.
Shard nothing for one match: 1 lakh seats is a small table. Spread events across databases, and keep each event's seats together.
Show seats left per block from a cache refreshed every second or so. It's always a little behind; the hold is the truth.

Open the line 30 minutes before sales. Everyone who joins by 12:00 gets a random position; people who join later go to the back in order. Being fast doesn't help, so bots refreshing at 11:59:59 gain nothing.
The token is signed and tied to the account, so it can't be forged or shared, and one account has one place.
Booking accepts only a signed admission token that expires after about 15 minutes. A call without one is refused, so nobody skips the line by calling the API directly.
Admit by what's left, not by the clock: when every seat is sold or held, stop admitting and tell everyone still in line it's sold out, with an option to wait for seats from holds that expire.
Show an honest position and a rough wait.
Verified phone number per account, and at most 4 tickets per account per match.
A challenge at line entry if the device or address looks automated; rate limits per account and per device.
Name on the ticket and ID checked at the gate for big matches, so bulk-bought tickets are hard to resell.
The QR code is signed by the server, so a scanner can tell a real ticket from a made-up one without asking anyone.
Each gate keeps the list of tickets already scanned for its stands and syncs with the others every few seconds. A stadium's network is busy on match day, so gates must work through short outages.
A second scan of the same ticket is flagged; a person decides, not the scanner.
Junior / mid: seat states, holding before payment, and a way to stop two people buying one seat.
Senior: holds with expiry in one conditional update, the crowd numbers leading to a waiting room, a cached seat map, per-account limits.
Lead: fairness (random order before opening), setting the admit rate from booking's capacity, assigning seats to cut contention, and gates that work offline.
"Payment arrives after the hold expired and the seats were resold." Refund at once and say so; the webhook must be safe to receive twice.
"The customer taps Pay twice, or the app retries." Each payment carries the order's idempotency key, so the provider charges once and the hold is confirmed once.
"The waiting room service dies." Positions are in signed tokens and the admitted-up-to number is saved, so a restarted service carries on as people poll; admitted tokens keep working.
"Two matches go on sale at the same minute." Separate lines and separate admit rates; each event's seats are in their own table or database.
"Why not just add servers?" The crowd is 50 times the seats. More servers serve more people a "sold out" faster; they don't make more seats.
"How would you test it?" Replay 1,000 holds for the same 10 seats at once and check exactly 10 are held, then let them expire and check the counts return.

body.x: The same match night from the other side: 3.5 crore people watching the stream. See how a CDN, and servers started before the toss, keep up when everyone arrives at once.
body.go: Try the IND vs PAK problem

practice.brief: Each test sends the crowd's requests: almost all of them are people in the line refreshing the waiting room or the "sold out" page, which is the same for everyone and may be five seconds old; one in two hundred is someone admitted from the line holding a seat. A hold is answered at once and must be done within a few minutes (half an hour when sales open at noon); two people must never hold the same seat, and no accepted hold may be lost.

steps.label: Holding the seat, if it is still free

tests.name: The waiting room
tests.desc: Someone in the line refreshes the waiting room for IND vs PAK.

tests.name: Hold seat N2-14-7
tests.desc: u1, admitted from the line, holds a free seat for 10 minutes; only one person can get it.

tests.name: The day before
tests.desc: 5,000 requests a second: people checking the stands and the sale time.

tests.name: The line forms
tests.desc: 2 lakh requests a second for an hour from 11 am: people in the line refreshing their place before sales open.

tests.name: Sales open at noon
tests.desc: For 15 minutes from 12:00, 10 lakh requests a second: everyone joins the line and refreshes. Only a few thousand a second can actually book. Holds may wait up to half an hour; none may be lost.

tests.name: A zone goes dark
tests.desc: At 11:10 am, with the line forming, one availability zone is lost for 15 minutes. Pages may slow down; holds may wait up to ten minutes and none may be lost.

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30. Holds may wait; none may be lost.

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (5,000 a second), storage and data transfer included. Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails.

wrong.name: No CDN
wrong.why: Every refresh of the waiting room reaches your servers: 2 lakh a second while the line forms.

wrong.name: Holds straight to the database
wrong.why: At noon 5,000 holds a second go straight to the database, far more than it takes.

wrong.name: Seats keyed by show
wrong.why: The seats table is keyed by the show alone: holding one seat reads every seat of the show.

wrong.name: Holds saved by a write-back cache
wrong.why: The seat holders write to a cache that saves to the database later: when it fails, holds people were told about are gone.

wrong.name: One zone
wrong.why: Every API server is in one zone: when it goes dark, nothing answers.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: No standby: when it crashes, holds wait 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: It passes every test, at several times the bill it needs.

mutantsAllowedWhy.remove:lb: The CDN may reach the Service group directly in this model.
mutantsAllowedWhy.engine:db:dynamodb: DynamoDB has conditional writes: holding a seat only if it is free works the same.
mutantsAllowedWhy.engine:db:cassandra: Cassandra holds a seat only if it is free with a lightweight transaction: as good for 5,000 holds a second.

fr.label: See the stands and seats left
A fair line (waiting room) when sales open
A seat is sold only once

est.label: Requests a second when sales open
est.how: 50 lakh people refreshing every few seconds

decisions.q: 50 lakh people arrive at 12:00 for 1 lakh seats. What do they hit?
options: The booking service itself, with extra servers added for the day
A waiting room that admits people at the rate booking can take
A rate limit that turns away anyone over the limit
decisions.why: Booking can only confirm so many seats a second, whatever the servers. A waiting room is fair and keeps it from falling over; a rate limit turns people away at random, and bots retry fastest.

decisions.q: How is a seat kept while someone pays?
options: Not held: whoever finishes paying first gets it
Held until the person closes the app, or until the sale is over
Held with an expiry in one atomic step, released if unpaid
decisions.why: Holding atomically means two people can't pick the same seat, and the expiry returns seats from abandoned payments. Not holding means paying for a seat that's gone; holding without expiry locks seats forever.

decisions.q: What finally stops the same seat being sold twice?
options: The database: a unique (show, seat) rule or a conditional update
The app greys out a seat as soon as anyone selects it
A check that the seat is still free just before the payment starts
decisions.why: The database itself refuses the second sale, so no bug or race elsewhere can double-sell a seat. A greyed-out seat and a check before payment can both be beaten by two people at the same instant.

hints.x: The sale is small (30,000 orders); the crowd is huge (50 lakh people). Which requirements protect each?
How many people can actually be shopping at once if a purchase takes 3 minutes? That, not the crowd, is your booking load.
Join a line (get a signed token), check your place, hold seats with an admitted token, then pay.
Most requests are people refreshing a waiting page or a "sold out" page. Who can answer those without your servers?
Put a CDN in front: 99% of the crowd is answered at the edge, so 10 lakh a second becomes 10,000 at your servers.
Booking can only go so fast. A Queue between the API servers and the booking workers is the line: it admits people at the rate the database can take.

Never sell a seat twice and never lose a hold: hold a seat only if it is still free, write it to a Multi-AZ database (not a cache that saves later), and keep API servers and seat holders in more than one zone.
